title: Always-on inference playbook: positioning brief
content:
One-pager purpose
This brief is a compact internal positioning piece to help GTM and product craft messaging that centers around one single customer need: keep LLM features up and predictable in production. It synthesizes mission, thesis, and the pragmatic value props teams care about when choosing an inference platform. Use this when writing one-pagers, sales notes, and brief product chapter intros.

Executive snapshot (2 lines)
Modern apps fail not because models are bad but because serving is brittle. Redwood makes inference 'always-on' by combining production-grade runtime controls, deterministic fallbacks, and cost-aware routing so teams hit availability and unit-economics targets simultaneously.

Mission statement
Enable engineering teams to ship LLM-powered features that stay online, within budget, and predictable at scale.

Thesis (what buyers are waking up to)
As open model variety and hardware complexity explode, the hard problem is no longer model quality but operational continuity. The companies that win will move from model ownership to serving mastery — those who can guarantee that critical user flows are low-latency, cost-predictable, and gracefully degrade under load.

Why Redwood (core narrative)
Redwood is built for the operational realities of production inference. We make serving deterministic: per-route SLOs, transparent unit cost accounting, and fallback policies that preserve product experience when a primary model or region becomes constrained. For engineering teams, that means fewer emergency rollbacks, predictable budgets, and faster risk-tolerant iterations.

Target customer pain (short list)
- Surprising outages during traffic spikes or model rollouts
- Unclear per-feature inference cost leading to budget blowouts
- Long debugging cycles when tail-latency or KV cache misses cause user-visible regressions
- Fear of deploying newer model variants due to lack of safe rollback mechanisms

How we solve it (value pillars mapped to buyer benefit)
- SLO-driven routing and per-route SLAs: enforce latency and availability targets at the route level so teams can own SLOs by feature, not by instance.  => Benefit: predictable user experience and simple incident math.
- Multi-variant fallbacks & compatibility matrix: automatic fallback to compatible model variants or lower-cost capacity tiers when primaries fail or saturate. => Benefit: graceful degradation instead of downtime.
- Cost-aware policies and visibility: token-level cost attribution, per-route heatmaps, and suggested batching/quantization profiles. => Benefit: predictable product economics and faster ops tuning.
- Deterministic caching and KV strategies: built-in prefix caching and cache hit diagnostics tailored to sequence distributions. => Benefit: reduced tail latency and lower token spend.
- Unified control plane across hosted/dedicated/private: same config, rollouts, and observability across environments. => Benefit: seamless migration and consistent ops playbooks.

Messaging pillars (short lines for copy)
- Always-on inference: keep features online, even when models change.
- Unit-economics as a first-class signal: measure and control cost per feature.
- Safe, gradual rollout as the default: ship risk-tolerantly with automated fallbacks.
- One runtime, many environments: dev-to-prod parity across hosted, dedicated, and private.

One-line positioning statements (audience variants)
- For engineers: "Ship LLM features that stay online — without firefighting at 2am."
- For platform leads: "A single control plane that turns inference variability into an ops SLA."
- For execs/finance: "Predictable inference costs and availability so your product roadmap is executable."

Evidence and proof points to use in collateral
- Runtime design: continuous batching + KV-aware caches reduce average per-token latency by X% (use specific benchmark callouts from Serving team).
- Fallback runway: can switch to compatible variants within <Y ms> under simulated saturation (reference internal chaos test ids).
- Customer outcomes: pilot customers reduced unexpected token spend by Z% after adopting cost-aware routing and per-route monitoring.

Competitive differentiation (how to talk about rivals without name-calling)
- Many vendors focus on model access or raw throughput; Redwood focuses on predictable product outcomes: SLOs, fallbacks, and per-route economics.
- Compared to self-hosting, Redwood offers a borrowable ops playbook and compatibility guarantees across regions and capacity profiles.
- Compared to simple managed endpoints, we expose operational levers (batching, cache, rollout policy) with guardrails so teams can optimize without risking uptime.

Practical GTM hooks (how to start conversations)
- "Do you have per-feature SLOs for your LLM flows?" (quick discovery that opens the door to discussing route-level observability)
- "Imagine a failed model rollout that auto-falls back instead of producing customer-facing errors." (use when presenting canary/rollback features)
- "Let’s map one high-cost route and show token-level cost impact in 30 minutes." (live demo hook for sales)

Short checklist for collateral and demos
- Demo: Canary a model update, trigger saturation, show automatic fallback and per-route incident timeline.
- One-pager: include a 'cost before/after' micro-case showing batching + cache impact.
- Slide: single diagram showing request routing policy (latency vs cost vs region) and where fallback sits.

Open questions and risks we should answer in product or GTM
- What are our quantified latency and failover SLAs at specific percentiles for flagship models? (ops to provide)
- What are standard compatibility matrices across model sizes/quantization profiles? (applied-ml to own)
- Which two early customers will we jointly publicize as always-on case studies for Q1? (sales & CS)

Usage guidance for teams
- Marketing: lean on the "always-on" theme but pair it with hard metrics (cost saved, SLOs met). Avoid generic words like "reliable" without numbers.
- Sales/SEs: open with a route-level discovery question and offer a quick cost/latency audit. Use the demo checklist above.
- Product: prioritize guardrails and observability hooks that make fallbacks auditable and reversible.

Next steps (owner: Go-to-market)
- Finalize two short customer narratives (1–2 paragraphs) that show uptime + cost improvements (due in 2 sprints).
- Create a demo script for the always-on scenario and rehearse with Solutions Engineering.
- Align with Serving and Applied-ML for three concrete benchmark numbers to include in public collateral.

Appendix: suggested soundbites
- "Downtime is a product decision — Redwood makes it one you can control."
- "Predictability, not just performance: know what a feature will cost and how it will behave before you ship it."
- "We treat fallbacks like features, not accidents."

End of brief
